title: Rational positive definite matrices are sums of rational outer squares
statement:
Use the rational and real fields $\mathbf Q,\mathbf R$ [def-weil-field]. Let $n\geq0$ be an integer and $H=(H_{ij})_{1\leq i,j\leq n}$ a symmetric matrix with entries in $\mathbf Q$, meaning $H_{ij}=H_{ji}$. Suppose its entrywise image in the real matrices is positive definite, meaning $\sum_{i,j}z_iH_{ij}z_j>0$ for every nonzero $z\in\mathbf R^n$. There are an integer $r\geq0$ and vectors $v_1,\ldots,v_r\in\mathbf Q^n$ such that
$$H_{ij}=\sum_{k=1}^r (v_k)_i(v_k)_j\qquad(1\leq i,j\leq n).$$
The equality is an equality of rational entries. The empty matrix $n=0$ is allowed, and $r=0$ denotes an empty sum.

source.place: Agent auxiliary for the split-real sum-of-squares argument: replacing a rational positive definite Gram matrix by rational rank-one squares. Milne II §1, proof of Lemma 1.3, printed pp.77–78 motivates the ambient algebra only; this matrix lemma is not asserted there. Agent proof recorded in report.md.

proof.text: If $n=0$, take $r=0$; there are no entry equalities to check. Otherwise put $V=\mathbf Q^n$ and $B(x,y)=\sum_{i,j}x_iH_{ij}y_j$. Finite distributivity makes $B$ rational bilinear, and the assumed symmetry of $H$ makes $B$ symmetric. The coordinate vectors give a finite basis of $V$. Apply [lem-sfb-rational-symmetric-form-orthogonal-basis] to obtain a finite basis $u_1,\ldots,u_s$ with $B(u_k,u_l)=0$ for $k\ne l$.

source.place: Agent proof of the rational Gram auxiliary, using the existing orthogonal-basis Mathlib leaf. Milne II §1, proof of Lemma 1.3, printed pp.77–78 motivates the parent algebra argument only and does not assert this matrix theorem.

proof.text: Put $d_k=B(u_k,u_k)\in\mathbf Q$. Each basis vector $u_k$ is nonzero, so at least one rational coordinate is nonzero and remains nonzero in $\mathbf R$. Applying the given real positive-definiteness inequality to that vector gives $d_k>0$. For each standard coordinate vector $e_i$ write its rational basis expansion $e_i=\sum_k c_{ki}u_k$, where $c_{ki}\in\mathbf Q$. Bilinearity and orthogonality give the rational identity $H_{ij}=B(e_i,e_j)=\sum_{k,l}c_{ki}c_{lj}B(u_k,u_l)=\sum_k d_k c_{ki}c_{kj}$.

source.place: Agent proof of the rational Gram auxiliary, using the existing orthogonal-basis Mathlib leaf. Milne II §1, proof of Lemma 1.3, printed pp.77–78 motivates the parent algebra argument only and does not assert this matrix theorem.

proof.text: For each $k$ write the positive rational $d_k=a_k/b_k$ with positive integers $a_k,b_k$ (its positive numerator and denominator suffice). Set $m_k=a_kb_k$. In $\mathbf Q$ the sum of $m_k$ copies of $1/b_k^2$ is $m_k/b_k^2=a_k/b_k=d_k$; the denominator is nonzero since $b_k>0$. Thus no rational square root of $d_k$ is required.

source.place: Agent proof of the rational Gram auxiliary, using the existing orthogonal-basis Mathlib leaf. Milne II §1, proof of Lemma 1.3, printed pp.77–78 motivates the parent algebra argument only and does not assert this matrix theorem.

proof.text: Index a finite family by the pairs $(k,t)$ with $1\le k\le s$ and $1\le t\le m_k$, and define its vectors by $(v_{k,t})_i=c_{ki}/b_k\in\mathbf Q$. Its size is $r=\sum_k m_k\ge0$; list these pairs in increasing $k$, then increasing $t$, to label the vectors $v_1,\ldots,v_r$. For every $i,j$, finite distributivity gives $\sum_{k,t}(v_{k,t})_i(v_{k,t})_j=\sum_k(m_k/b_k^2)c_{ki}c_{kj}=\sum_k d_kc_{ki}c_{kj}=H_{ij}$. These are rational entry equalities, as required.
